newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Prescott questions pace of change.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Prescott questions pace of change.

text.p: Britain's deputy Labour Party leader has questioned the pace of change in his party as it bids to modernise its policies and regain power after 17 years in opposition.
In an interview with The Times newspaper, published on Saturday, deputy leader John Prescott said he admired and respected leader Tony Blair but expressed unease about too much reform, too soon.
"Tony's very strongly of the view that you just don't stop. He wants to keep the party adjusting. I think he's right about that. The real problem is: how far do you go without derailing?
"Sometimes you can go too fast. It will hit the bloody wall, the buffers. The more and more you pile on the change, the more and more people feel a little uneasy," Prescott was quoted as saying.

Blair has sought to capture the middle ground of politics, ditching his party's long-standing commitment to nationalisation of major industries and seeing to re-evaluate Labour's traditionally close relationship with trade unions.
Labour now enjoys a 20 point lead over the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls just eight months before Britain must hold a general election.

The interview with Prescott, a former trade union leader, was published two days before the Labour Party annual conference, where the party is expected to come under attack from left-wingers over workers' rights and pensions.
Prescott said he frequently disagreed with Blair's views.
"I used to sit with him on a committee in the national executive and some of his views were pretty unacceptable to most of us," Prescott said.
Asked to specify, he added; "Well there were some views he had about trade unions." Prescott declined to give details.

Prescott made clear however that he liked and admired Blair. "I"ve got quite a lot of respect for Tony Blair. He's been a tremendous force in British politics. I admire anybody who argues his case," he said.
Blair faces the real prospect of embarrassing defeats at the Labour Conference, which opens on Monday in the northern town of Blackpool.

Baroness Barbara Castle, 85, a leading figure in Labour governments in the 1960s and 1970s, has spearheaded a campaign to commit the party restore a link between the state retirement pension and average earnings.
But Labour, fearful of being tagged by the ruling Conservatives as taxers and spenders, wants instead to provide the 700,000 neediest pensioners with a top-up to their pension entitlement.
Castle, who established the link between pensions and earnings when she was a cabinet minister, has vowed to take her fight to the conference floor.
Castle said she wanted Blair to win the election but warned that his rush to capture the middle ground could backfire.

"What's happening is that we're becoming more and more indistinguishable from the Tories (Conservatives). And if you think that's the way to win the election, I think it's a gross mis-estimate of what's happening.
"And remember, I've been through every general election since the war...I've seen the tactics fail," Castle said.
